title: Bhutan on a budget: SDF, costs and savings
meta_description: What Bhutan really costs in 2026: SDF for Indians and other nationals, guide and vehicle costs, hotels, food, and how to travel for ₹4,500–6,500 a day.
summary: For Indian nationals, Bhutan on a budget costs about ₹4,500–6,500 per person a day: ₹1,200 SDF, a simple certified hotel, a share of a guide and vehicle, and local food. Enter by road from Siliguri and travel in a group of four to six. Most other nationals pay USD 100 a night SDF.

sections.heading: How Bhutan's costs work
paras: Bhutan prices tourism differently from its neighbours. Every visitor pays a Sustainable Development Fee, or SDF, for each night in the country, and every tourist must travel with a licensed guide beyond the first checkpoint. Those two rules shape every budget, and they are why a cheap trip to Bhutan looks different from a cheap trip to Sikkim or Nepal.

As we understand the rules in 2026, Indian nationals pay an SDF of ₹1,200 (Nu 1,200) per person per night. Most other nationalities pay USD 100 per person per night, a reduced rate that the government has said runs until 31 August 2027. Children aged 6 to 12 pay half and under-6s pay nothing. Bangladeshi and Maldivian nationals have also had their own rates. These rules have changed several times since 2022 and can change again, so check current status before you travel.

After the SDF, the big costs are the guide and the vehicle, which cost the same whether one person or six share them. Hotels, food and entry fees come next. Unlike in much of the Himalaya, you cannot cut costs by sleeping in the cheapest guesthouse in town or hitchhiking between valleys, because tourists must use certified stays and travel with their guide. The savings come from how you arrive, how many people share, and when you go.

sections.heading: Road or air: the biggest choice
paras: Most budget travellers from India come by road. Reach Siliguri by train to New Jalpaiguri or by flight to Bagdogra, then take a bus or shared jeep about 160 km and 4–5 hours to Jaigaon, for ₹150–400 a seat. Walk through the Bhutan Gate into Phuentsholing, where your guide meets you. From there it is about 150 km and 5–6 hours to Thimphu.

Flying into Paro is faster and gives a famous view of the peaks, but one-way fares from Indian cities often cost ₹8,000–20,000, and the road trip back adds two long days. For a group of five, flying both ways can cost as much as the rest of a saver trip combined.

The road has costs of its own: two long travel days of 5–6 hours each between Phuentsholing and Thimphu or Paro, and one more night of SDF and hotel. On a 6-night trip, that still saves most travellers ₹15,000–35,000 per person compared with return flights.

sections.heading: Sharing a guide and vehicle
paras: A licensed guide and a tourist vehicle with driver together often cost ₹6,000–10,000 a day. That is a heavy load for one traveller, a manageable one for two, and a small share for six. This is why budget trips in Bhutan are almost always small groups.

If you are a family of four or more, or a group of friends, you can book a private trip and get the shared rate. Solo travellers can join small-group departures run by licensed operators. As we understand it, you can stay in Phuentsholing town without a guide, but you need one to go further. Check current status before you travel.
list: Groups of 4–6 fit one SUV or small van with luggage.
Agree the route before you arrive: each district beyond Paro and Thimphu must be on your route permit.
Ask whether your guide fee covers their meals and room; on most trips it does.

sections.heading: Beds, food and fees
paras: Tourists must stay in accommodation certified by the Department of Tourism. Simple certified hotels in Thimphu, Paro and Punakha cost about ₹2,500–4,500 a night for a double, which is ₹1,250–2,250 each on twin share. Heating varies at this level, so ask. In Haa and Phobjikha, registered farmhouse homestays cost about ₹2,000–3,500 per person with dinner and breakfast and are often the best value in the country.
Eat where drivers and office workers eat. A plate of ema datshi, the chilli and cheese stew, with red rice and dal costs ₹200–400 in a local restaurant; momos ₹120–250. Hotel buffets cost far more.

Entry fees add up. Major dzongs, Taktsang, Buddha Dordenma and museums charge tourist fees, from a few hundred to a couple of thousand ngultrum each. Budget ₹4,000–6,000 in total for a 6-night western circuit, and check current status before you travel, as the fee list has been revised more than once.

sections.heading: Ten ways to spend less
paras: These are the savings that make a real difference, roughly in order of size.
list: Use an Indian passport or voter ID if you have one; Indian nationals pay a far lower SDF than most other visitors.
Enter by road through Phuentsholing instead of flying into Paro.
Travel in a group of four to six to share the guide and vehicle.
Keep the trip to the western valleys; each extra district adds nights of every cost.
Visit from late November to February outside festival dates, when many hotels drop rates.
Choose farmhouse homestays in Haa or Phobjikha for a night or two.
Eat local food at local prices.
Apply for your entry permit online before travel so you do not lose half a day at the Phuentsholing office.
Buy a local B-Mobile or TashiCell SIM instead of paying Indian roaming rates.
Carry rupees in ₹100–500 notes; they are accepted at par with the ngultrum in most places.

sections.heading: What a saver trip costs in total
paras: Our 6-night saver trip from Siliguri, covering Phuentsholing, Thimphu, Punakha and Paro, starts at ₹34,500 per person for Indian nationals in a group of five or six. Our 7-night version with two farmhouse nights in Phobjikha starts at ₹40,000. Both include SDF, simple hotels, a shared vehicle and licensed guide, breakfast and dinner, but not travel to Siliguri, lunches or entry fees.

For non-Indian nationals, the same trips cost much more because of the SDF: USD 100 a night comes to roughly ₹50,000 or more per person over 6 nights at 2026 exchange rates, against ₹7,200 for an Indian national, plus a visa fee. For most international visitors, Bhutan is not a budget country, but sharing and travelling in winter still cut costs.

faqs.q: How much does a Bhutan trip cost for Indians?
faqs.a: On a budget, about ₹4,500–6,500 per person a day, including ₹1,200 SDF, a simple hotel on twin share, a share of the guide and vehicle and local meals. A 6-night road trip from Siliguri starts at about ₹34,500 per person in a group. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the SDF for Indian tourists?
faqs.a: As we understand it, ₹1,200 (Nu 1,200) per person per night, paid with the entry permit. Children 6–12 pay half and under-6s are exempt. It has applied since Bhutan reopened to tourists in 2022, and the wider SDF rules have been revised since, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the SDF for foreign tourists?
faqs.a: Most non-Indian nationals pay USD 100 per person per night, as we understand the current rule, which the government has said runs to 31 August 2027. It was USD 200 when the new policy began in 2022. Children 6–12 pay half. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I travel in Bhutan without a guide?
faqs.a: Not beyond the first checkpoint, as we understand the 2024 tourism rules, for Indian or other nationals. You can stay in Phuentsholing town without one. Guides must be licensed by the Department of Tourism. Check current status before you travel, as enforcement details have changed.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to enter Bhutan by road or air?
faqs.a: By road, for most Indian travellers. A shared jeep or bus from Siliguri to Jaigaon costs ₹150–400, against ₹8,000–20,000 for a one-way flight into Paro. The road adds two long travel days and one more night of costs, but still saves money overall.

faqs.q: How much money should I carry in Bhutan?
faqs.a: For a 6-night saver trip with SDF, hotel, guide and vehicle prepaid, carry ₹8,000–15,000 per person in cash for lunches, entry fees not included, drinks, shopping and tips. Indian rupee notes up to ₹500 are widely accepted. ATMs and card acceptance are patchy outside Thimphu and Paro.

As we understand the rules, children under 6 pay no SDF and children aged 6 to 12 pay half, for Indian and other nationals alike. Older children pay the full rate. Carry birth certificates or passports as proof of age. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I stay in homestays in Bhutan?
faqs.a: Yes, in registered farmhouse homestays, which are certified for tourists. Haa and Phobjikha have the most. They cost about ₹2,000–3,500 per person with dinner and breakfast and are among the best-value nights in Bhutan. Bathrooms may be shared.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest month to visit Bhutan?
faqs.a: Late November to February outside festival dates, and the monsoon months of June to August. Many hotels drop rates then. Winter is cold but clear; monsoon brings landslides and cloud. The SDF stays the same all year, so savings come from hotels.
